title: These Days, "Making Games Entirely with AI" Is Nothing More Than a Scam for Views
author: According_North_5662
selftext:
Recently, I've seen countless people claiming that they have absolutely no background in programming or 3D modeling, yet have managed to create amazing games — even supposedly AAA-quality titles — using nothing but AI.

They post short gameplay videos on X, some of which look visually stunning. And countless people jump on the bandwagon, claiming these games could easily sell for $10–20 on Steam, or that these AI-generated games are better than many games made entirely by human developers. Some even declare that traditional game developers are doomed.

It's frustrating to watch. But here's the problem: **They're all lying.**

Take this project, for example: [https://littleprince.dev/](https://littleprince.dev/)

It has attracted millions of views on X, along with an overwhelming amount of praise.

But the reality is that most of the people praising this project haven't even clicked the link, let alone actually played the game. They're simply following the hype and reposting what everyone else is saying.

Whenever I asked them, "Have you actually played this game?" not a single person answered. Complete silence.

**Well, I have. I've played through the entire thing.**

If someone told me this was an interactive animated story designed for five-year-old children, I might actually think it was pretty decent.

But if you expected me to pay money for this as a video game, I would absolutely request a refund within five minutes.

Here's why:

**1. Terrible performance.**

The game suffers from severe stuttering and runs nowhere near smoothly. My laptop has a Ryzen 9 8945HX and an RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, yet the performance is still noticeably poor. There's simply no sense of fluidity.

**2. Unnatural character animations.**

The skeletal animations are bizarre. The characters move in ways that are clearly inconsistent with natural human biomechanics.

**3. Modeling errors everywhere.**

The environments are full of obvious 3D modeling issues. For example, curtains clip straight through walls. Problems like this are scattered throughout the game.

**4. Almost nonexistent gameplay.**

The only meaningful interaction in the entire game happens in the first level, where you pick up a watering can, fill it with water, and water some flowers.

After that, practically all you can do is talk to NPCs.

And by "talk," I don't mean actual dialogue interactions. There are no dialogue choices whatsoever. You simply watch a few lines of predetermined text appear on the screen.

There are eight levels in total, with approximately ten conversations.

**That's it. That's the entire game.**

Let me give you another example.

In the second level, you arrive at a new location. There's an NPC standing there. You walk up to the NPC, trigger a conversation, read a few lines of scripted dialogue, and then it's over.

The level is complete.

Yes, that's literally the entire second level.

Every level follows essentially the same pattern.

**There is no actual gameplay.**

It's nothing more than a fairy tale presented through 3D models. The experience is almost identical to watching an animated movie, except you have a controllable character that can wander around the environment.

That's all.

The entire experience takes approximately ten minutes to complete.

And yet, influencers and content creators are calling this a game and showering it with praise so exaggerated that the exact same compliments wouldn't sound out of place if they were describing The Legend of Zelda.

To make matters worse, the person behind this project started taking advertisements and publishing game development tutorials the very next day.

It's increasingly obvious to me that the entire point was to generate views, attract attention, and capitalize on the hype — not to genuinely create a worthwhile video game.

**This isn't a revolution in game development. It's a traffic-generating scheme built around AI hype.**

**They're all frauds.**

comments.author: Post-reality
comments.body:
Unless you build casual games, copycats or remakes of old games - it's impossible to create a game in a short period of time. I am almost 450 hours into my game development time, and I expect that time to cross into 10,000+ hours by the time of the closed beta release. Sounds bad, but that game would have costed at least several millions to develop years ago, while now it's a fraction of that.

The whole hype reminds me of Dall E 2 back in 2022, as people would be blown out and obsess over images model generating capabilities, with prompts such as "a photo of a 13 years old child from 1900 using a smartphone", or "a photo taken by a Nokia phone, circa 2005" - eventually the hype will wear off and the grifters will move on to the next scheme.
